subject: Aerial surveys with wide ranging ESW from year to year

messages.author: ba840c21971f1ac1
messages.subject: Aerial surveys with wide ranging ESW from year to year
parts:
We have used line transect survey methods to survey white-tailed deer in 3 =
study areas in South Florida. Our density estimates have varied widely ov=
er the last 3 years and I am hoping to obtain some guidance on how to proce=
ed.

The survey areas are large (avg. 200 km2) and surveys are conducted using h=
elicopters. The transects are placed in a parallel systematic grid at 1 km=
intervals. Distances are recorded in bins (0-25m, 25-50m, 50-100m, etc. =
up to 250+ meters). In general, visibility is good, although there are por=
tions where the line is not visible due to thicker habitat.

Using one area as an example, the number of observations (clusters of deer)=
have not changed much in the past years (143 to 179), however the abundanc=
e estimate has fluctuated from 810 deer in 2009 to 176 deer in 2011. The r=
eason for this seems to be a change in the Effective Strip Width, which was=
71 meters in 2009 and 300 meters (our cut off value) in 2011. In 2009, t=
he histogram had a nice shoulder near the line, in 2010 there was some shou=
lder, and in 2011 the shape of the detection function was basically a strai=
ght line. The pattern ; with very narrow ESW the first survey year and the=
300 m ESW is seen in the other 2 areas also. The overall number of observ=
ations has not changed much, basically just where the deer, in relation to =
the transect, are observed has changed.

Aerial surveys have been historically used in these areas due to large size=
of the areas, low deer density, high visibility and inaccessibility by oth=
er means. Aircraft used, observers, field methods (e.g. the way observers=
search for deer, concentrating on the line) or visibility due to habitat h=
ave not changed in the past 3 years.

We don't want to give up on line transect survey methods, but at this point=
it is difficult to use the data for management decisions. We don't believ=
e that there has been a drastic change in the deer population in these area=
, in fact harvest numbers have increased in the last 3 years. Could this d=
ue simply to sample size? It seems odd that by chance alone all 3 areas wou=
ld experience this shift in deer location (transects were created using GIS=
and do not follow any landscape patterns).

Has anyone experienced something similar? Any advice on how to proceed or =
anything we can change in our field methods or analyses to try to come up w=
ith a better estimate. We are considering mapping the sections of transects=
where visibility is very low and eliminating those sections out of our sur=
vey, but I don't believe that would help us with our ESW issue.

Thank you,
Elina Garrison

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: Aerial surveys with wide ranging ESW from year to year
parts:
Elina, with those sample sizes, I think you need to be considering the assu=
mptions, and what may be going wrong. So:

1. How are distances estimated? Are counts by distance bin reliable? (i.=
e. are animals reliably allocated to distance bin?) Has anything changed o=
ver the 3 years in how distances are estimated?

2. Do animals respond to the helicopter before their distance band is reco=
rded? Has anything changed in those 3 years so that responsive movement is=
causing greater bias in year 3 than in year 1?

3. Have you had the same observers in all 3 years? Have they searched in =
the same way each year (e.g. looking ahead of the helicopter, to detect ani=
mals before they move away from the helicopter vs. searching to the side, a=
nd only recording animals after responsive movement has started)?

4. Your last band is '250+ m', yet you say you used w=3D300m. Might obser=
vers have been recording animals beyond 300 m in 2011? W=3D250m might be a=
more reliable choice.

5. Are animals culled by helicopter? If so, is this a recent change? (It=
might result in animals responding by fleeing from the helicopter, and hen=
ce being recorded too far from the line after responsive movement has occur=
red, in 2011.)

If sample sizes are typically over 100 per year in each area, and you're se=
eing a consistent increase in ESW over the 3 years in each area, I agree th=
at this will not be due to sample size. You need to understand what is cha=
nging to cause this ...

Steve

messages.author: caaac2dc0aae28b8
messages.subject: Re: Aerial surveys with wide ranging ESW from year to year
parts:
Elina;
I wonder if a change in aircraft or pilot could explain some of this? In m=
y experience, it is not possible to see directly below a helicopter, and th=
us the center line must be shifted to account for this. If you changed hel=
icopters this might have changed the distance required for this adjustment.=
Also, the altitude of the survey must be steady if you are assuming a fix=
ed altitude in your calculations of the distance. If a new pilot is not go=
od at holding the correct altitude this could introduce bias in the distanc=
e estimates.
Eric
